c.tagline: Golden domes, grand boulevards, and a metro built like an underground palace.

taxi.fareNote: Most rides booked via Yandex Go app with upfront fixed pricing; street-hailed taxis are rare and best avoided due to overcharging.

emergency.note: 112 is the universal emergency number reachable from any phone, including without SIM/credit.

avoid.reason: Central Moscow is safe; distant dormitory districts like Biryulyovo and Golyanovo have rougher reputations at night and hold nothing for visitors.
Watch for pickpockets on the metro and around Red Square and Arbat, use official ride-hail apps rather than street taxis, and carry your passport for police checks.

hood_desc: Grand imperial core packed with the Kremlin, Red Square and Bolshoi Theatre; best for first-time visitors who want everything within walking distance, at premium prices.
Moscow's most romantic pedestrian street lined with cafes, street art, and old mansions; ideal for culture lovers who want charm and easy metro access without being right on Red Square.
Trendy arts district built around a former chocolate factory with galleries, bars, and coworking spaces; suits younger travelers and creatives who want a hip, walkable scene.
Upscale, leafy residential area near Gorky Park and the river with boutique hotels and embassies; good for those wanting a quieter, elegant base near green space and museums.
Historic merchant quarter across the river from the Kremlin with Tretyakov Gallery and quiet courtyards; suits travelers wanting authentic local feel with skyline views and value.

water.note: Officially meets sanitary standards, but most residents avoid drinking it raw; bottled water is the safer choice for visitors.

transit.pay: Visitors typically buy a Troika contactless smart card, sold and topped up at metro kiosks and machines, valid across metro, MCC, MCD, tram and bus. Bank contactless cards and phone payment (Mir Pay) are also accepted directly at metro turnstiles.
transit.hours: Metro runs approximately 5:30am-1:00am daily; no regular all-night service, though some New Year's Eve exceptions apply.
transit.note: The Moscow Metro is famed for its ornate Stalin-era station architecture and is one of the busiest and most efficient systems in the world.

train: Sapsan high-speed rail to St. Petersburg
Long-distance trains from 9 mainline stations (e.g. Leningradsky, Kazansky, Yaroslavsky)
bus: Intercity coaches from Central Bus Station
ferry: Seasonal river cruises/water shuttles on the Moskva River

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up or leaving 5-10% at restaurants is appreciated but not expected everywhere.

food.name: Pelmeni
food.desc: Small Siberian dumplings of minced meat in thin dough, boiled and eaten with sour cream, butter and black pepper or vinegar.

places.name: Lepim i Varim
places.note: Hand-folded dumplings in a scruffy-cool room; the reason Moscow's pelmeni revival happened.

places.name: Grand Cafe Dr. Zhivago
places.note: Round-the-clock Soviet-glamour dining room opposite the Kremlin; strong on all the classics.

places.name: Varenichnaya No.1
places.note: Retro 1960s apartment styling, cheap plates of pelmeni and vareniki, several branches.

food.name: Blini
food.desc: Thin yeasted pancakes rolled around sour cream, curd cheese, mushrooms, salmon or caviar. Eaten year round and by the pile at Maslenitsa.

places.name: Grand Cafe Dr. Zhivago
places.note: Blini with red caviar and sour cream served all day and night.

places.name: Cafe Pushkin
places.note: 19th-century mansion setting for the grand version, best with the caviar service.

places.name: Teremok
places.note: Fast-food chain that got blini right; the cheapest reliable pancake in Moscow.

food.name: Borscht
food.desc: Deep-red beetroot and beef soup finished with a spoonful of smetana and eaten with garlic bread rolls.

places.name: Cafe Pushkin
places.note: Old-world dining rooms and a textbook borscht; the ground-floor cafe is the affordable way in.

places.name: Mari Vanna
places.note: Set up like a Soviet grandmother's flat, with the home cooking to match.

places.name: Grand Cafe Dr. Zhivago
places.note: Serves borscht 24 hours, handy after a late night or an early train.

food.name: Olivier salad
food.desc: The Russian New Year staple, invented in Moscow: potato, egg, peas, pickles and meat bound in mayonnaise.

places.name: Cafe Pushkin
places.note: Serves a refined version close to the 19th-century Hermitage restaurant original.

places.name: Grand Cafe Dr. Zhivago
places.note: Nostalgic Soviet plating and a strong list of zakuski to go alongside.

places.name: Mari Vanna
places.note: The homemade version, exactly as it appears on a Russian family table.

food.name: Beef Stroganoff
food.desc: Strips of beef in a mustard and sour cream sauce, named for a St Petersburg count but on every Moscow classic menu.

places.name: Cafe Pushkin
places.note: Traditional preparation served with crisp potato straws in a grand library room.

places.name: White Rabbit
places.note: Glass-domed rooftop restaurant famous for modern Russian cooking and city views; book well ahead.

places.name: Grand Cafe Dr. Zhivago
places.note: Reliable classic version at a fraction of the fine-dining price.

food.name: Syrniki
food.desc: Little pan-fried curd-cheese pancakes dusted with sugar and served with sour cream and jam. The Russian breakfast.

places.name: Grand Cafe Dr. Zhivago
places.note: Widely rated the best syrniki in the city, served from breakfast onwards.

places.name: Mari Vanna
places.note: Homestyle syrniki with condensed milk in a deliberately cluttered living-room setting.

places.name: Danilovsky Market
places.note: Food hall counters do breakfast syrniki cheaply among the produce stalls.

food.name: Vodka
food.desc: Drunk cold in shots with zakuski: pickles, herring, black bread and salo. Never sipped and never mixed at a Russian table.

places.name: Cafe Pushkin
places.note: Long list of premium and house-infused vodkas with a proper zakuski spread.

places.name: Mari Vanna
places.note: Homemade infusions in horseradish, cranberry and honey pepper, poured from decanters.

places.name: Grand Cafe Dr. Zhivago
places.note: Flights of infused vodka served at any hour with caviar and pickles.

food.name: Kvass
food.desc: Barely alcoholic fermented rye-bread drink, tart and slightly fizzy. Sold from street tankers in summer and used to make cold okroshka soup.

places.name: Danilovsky Market
places.note: Traditional-style kvass on tap among the food-hall stalls, plus fresh berry morse.

places.name: Depo Moskva
places.note: Huge food hall in a former tram depot with craft kvass and everything else.

places.name: Teremok
places.note: Cheapest way to try kvass and mors, poured alongside the blini counter.

landmarks: Saint Basil's Cathedral
Its riot of colorful onion domes on Red Square makes it the single most photographed building in Russia.
Moscow Kremlin
The fortified medieval citadel and seat of Russian power, with its red walls and gold-domed cathedrals, anchors the city's skyline.
Red Square
The vast historic square linking the Kremlin, GUM, and St. Basil's offers Moscow's most iconic wide-angle shot.
GUM Department Store
This grand 19th-century glass-roofed arcade on Red Square is a stunning example of ornate Russian retail architecture, especially lit up at night.
Bolshoi Theatre
The neoclassical home of Russian ballet and opera, fronted by its famous quadriga statue, is a beloved architectural landmark.
Spasskaya Tower
The Kremlin's most famous gate tower, topped with a glowing red star and clock, is a symbol recognized worldwide.
Cathedral of Christ the Saviour
The world's tallest Orthodox church, rebuilt after Soviet demolition, is a gleaming white-and-gold riverside landmark.
Moscow State University Main Building
One of Stalin's Seven Sisters skyscrapers, this soaring tower is a striking monument to Soviet-era architecture.
Ostankino Tower
Once the tallest freestanding structure in the world, this needle-like TV tower dominates the Moscow skyline.
Novodevichy Convent
A UNESCO-listed 16th-century fortified convent with striking red-and-white towers beside a scenic pond.

train.note: All trains to the EU (Helsinki, Warsaw, Berlin, Paris, the Baltics) remain suspended because of the war and sanctions, and the Beijing/Ulaanbaatar through trains have not returned; a twice-monthly Pyongyang sleeper resumed in 2025 but is effectively unbookable for Western travellers. Central Asian sleepers (including Dushanbe, resumed June 2026, and Tashkent) use Kazansky station; Belarus trains use Belorussky. Note rzd.ru is usually geo-blocked outside Russia.

bus.note: Most Western coach operators withdrew from Russia after 2022; Ecolines is the main survivor for EU-bound travel, with long checks at the Latvian border. Buses to Minsk and the Caucasus leave from the Severnye Vorota and Salaryevo terminals.

ferry.note: Moscow is deep inland with no international passenger sailings. River cruises on the Volga–Baltic network are domestic only, and pre-war Baltic Sea ferries from St Petersburg remain suspended.

half.name: Sergiev Posad
half.blurb: The Golden Ring's spiritual heart, crowned by the blue-and-gold Trinity Lavra monastery complex.

half.name: Kolomna
half.blurb: A riverside old town with a white kremlin, onion domes and famous local pastila sweets.

half.name: Borodino
half.blurb: The vast battlefield where Napoleon met the Russian army, now a monument-dotted historic field.

half.name: Tula
half.blurb: Famed for its kremlin, armaments museum, gingerbread and samovars, plus Tolstoy's estate nearby.

half.name: Abramtsevo
half.blurb: A wooded country estate turned artists' colony that inspired generations of Russian painters and craftsmen.

full.name: Rostov Veliky
full.blurb: An ancient lakeside town whose photogenic kremlin and monasteries anchor the Golden Ring route.
